knowledgePoints.name: Code that runs vs. a request that might be honoured
knowledgePoints.teach:
Programmatic enforcement guarantees deterministic compliance; prompt instructions are probabilistic and have a non-zero failure rate.

A hook is code that runs. A prompt is a request. If a rule must hold on every run — including the ones nobody is watching — it belongs in a hook.

This is the answer to the exam's most-quoted sample question. An agent skips get_customer in 12% of cases before issuing refunds. The fix is a programmatic prerequisite that blocks lookup_order and process_refund until identity is verified — not more few-shot examples, not a stronger instruction, not a better model.

Twelve percent is not a prompting problem. Twelve percent is what "usually" looks like at scale.

questions.q: Production data shows that in 12% of cases, your customer support agent skips get_customer entirely before calling process_refund, using only the customer's stated name to identify the account. This has led to several refunds issued to the wrong customer. Which change would most reliably close this gap?
options: Add a programmatic prerequisite that blocks process_refund until get_customer has returned a verified customer ID.
Update the system prompt to state explicitly that identity verification is mandatory before any refund is processed.
Add few-shot examples to the system prompt showing the agent always calling get_customer before process_refund.
Switch to a larger model with stronger instruction-following to reduce the rate of skipped steps.
questions.explain: A programmatic prerequisite guarantees the sequence holds on every run, closing the gap entirely rather than reducing it. Options B and C are both prompt-based fixes that rely on probabilistic compliance — they might cut the 12% rate but can't eliminate it. Option D assumes model capability is the bottleneck, but the failure is a missing enforcement mechanism, not a comprehension problem.

questions.q: Your support agent's system prompt already states that identity must be verified via get_customer before any refund is authorized, but production logs still show occasional refunds processed without that call ever happening. The team is deciding which of several policies to enforce with a hook instead of leaving them in the prompt. Which policy is the best candidate for hook enforcement?
options: Requiring the agent to keep a warm, empathetic tone whenever a customer's message reads as frustrated or dissatisfied.
Blocking any call to process_refund until get_customer has returned a verified customer identity for that account.
Requiring the agent to summarize any document longer than a few paragraphs before quoting specific passages from it.
Requiring the agent to ask a clarifying question whenever a customer's request is ambiguous about which order it concerns.
questions.explain: Verifying identity before a refund is a hard invariant that must hold on every run, which is exactly what a hook enforces deterministically. Keeping a warm tone with frustrated customers, deciding when a document needs summarizing, and recognizing when a request is ambiguous are judgment calls the model is well suited to make, not invariants that need programmatic gating.

reviewQuestions.q: A team is debating whether a new 'never log a customer's full card number' rule should live only in the agent's system prompt or also be enforced by a hook. One engineer summarizes the general distinction between the two mechanisms for the rest of the team. Which summary is accurate?
options: Hooks execute in a separate process, so they run measurably faster than a prompt instruction the model reads on every turn.
Prompts should be phased out entirely in favor of hooks wherever a hook could technically be written to enforce the rule.
A hook is code that runs deterministically every time its event fires; a prompt is only a request the model may or may not follow.
Hooks exist only to gate tool calls, while prompts remain the sole mechanism for shaping what the model writes in its response.
reviewQuestions.explain: A hook is code that executes on every occurrence of its event, giving a guarantee a prompt cannot provide. The claim about execution speed conflates a different property with the real distinction, phasing prompts out entirely ignores that judgment calls still belong there, and restricting hooks to tool-call gating undersells what hooks can observe and enforce across other events like Stop or UserPromptSubmit.

knowledgePoints.name: The event list
knowledgePoints.teach:
Python HookEvent: PreToolUse, PostToolUse, PostToolUseFailure, UserPromptSubmit, Stop, SubagentStop, PreCompact, Notification, SubagentStart, PermissionRequest. The TypeScript SDK supports additional events beyond these.

Group them by what they are about and the list stops being a list:

  • Per tool call — PreToolUse, PostToolUse, PostToolUseFailure, PermissionRequest
  • Per turn — UserPromptSubmit, Stop, SubagentStop
  • Per agent / session — SubagentStart, PreCompact, Notification

questions.q: You are building a compliance check that requires the agent to have cited at least one source before it is allowed to finish responding to the user, and the check needs to run every single time the agent attempts to end its turn. Which hook event should the check subscribe to?
options: PostToolUse, so the check runs immediately after each individual tool result is returned to the model.
Notification, so the check runs whenever the SDK surfaces a user-facing notification during the session.
SessionEnd, so the check runs only once the entire multi-turn session with the user has fully concluded.
Stop, so the check runs when the agent attempts to end its turn, letting it require a citation before allowing that.
questions.explain: Stop fires specifically when the agent attempts to end its turn, which is what makes it the right place to require a citation before that is allowed. PostToolUse fires per tool call rather than per turn, Notification is for informational events, and SessionEnd — even where it exists — fires only once the whole session is already over, too late to gate a single turn.

questions.q: A tool call to a payment gateway throws an exception, and you want a dedicated hook to run recovery logic specifically for that failure, without adding failure-handling branches to your existing PostToolUse success-path code. Which event should the recovery hook subscribe to?
options: PostToolUse, since it fires for every tool call regardless of whether the call succeeded or failed.
PostToolUseFailure, a dedicated event that fires specifically when a tool call has already failed.
PermissionRequest, since it fires whenever a tool call requires explicit authorization before running.
UserPromptSubmit, since it fires before the model begins processing a new request from the user.
questions.explain: PostToolUseFailure is a distinct event dedicated to calls that have already failed, so recovery logic can live in its own handler instead of being threaded through the success path. PostToolUse does not fire for failed calls, PermissionRequest concerns authorization rather than outcome, and UserPromptSubmit fires before the tool call happens at all.

reviewQuestions.q: While reviewing the SDK's hook documentation, a colleague claims there is a Python HookEvent called ToolResultReceived that fires whenever a tool returns output. You check the actual list of events to confirm. Which statement is correct?
options: ToolResultReceived exists and fires before PostToolUse specifically for read-only tools such as Read and Grep.
ToolResultReceived exists but only fires for tool calls that originate from within a subagent.
ToolResultReceived does not exist; PostToolUse is the actual event that fires when a tool call completes.
ToolResultReceived exists and replaced PostToolUse in the most recent version of the Python HookEvent list.
reviewQuestions.explain: ToolResultReceived is not one of the Python HookEvent values; PostToolUse is the actual event that fires once a tool call completes, whether by success or via the separate PostToolUseFailure event. The other claims all describe behavior for an event that was never part of the list to begin with.

knowledgePoints.name: HookMatcher and the callback signature
knowledgePoints.teach:
Hooks go in the hooks option, keyed by event, as a list of matchers:

HookMatcher(
    matcher="Bash",        # tool name or pattern, e.g. "Write|Edit"; omit to match all
    hooks=[my_callback],
    timeout=None,          # seconds; default 600, except UserPromptSubmit at 30
)

The callback is (input, tool_use_id, context) -> HookJSONOutput. input is a discriminated union on hook_event_name.

All hook inputs share session_id, transcript_path, cwd and an optional permission_mode. PreToolUseHookInput adds tool_name, tool_input, tool_use_id — and, when firing inside a subagent, agent_id and agent_type.

questions.q: You want a hook registered under PreToolUse to run whenever the agent calls Write or Edit, but not when it calls Read, and you want to express that directly through the HookMatcher's matcher field rather than filtering inside the callback itself. How should you write the matcher?
options: Set matcher to the list ["Write", "Edit"], since HookMatcher accepts an array of exact tool names.
Set matcher to the comma-separated string "Write,Edit" and let the SDK split it into individual tool names.
Leave matcher unset entirely and add an early return inside the callback whenever tool_name is not Write or Edit.
Set matcher to the pattern string "Write|Edit", which HookMatcher parses as matching either tool name.
questions.explain: HookMatcher's matcher field accepts a pattern string like "Write|Edit", which the framework parses as matching either tool name for that hook. An array of exact names and a comma-separated string are not the formats the field expects, and leaving matcher unset would run the hook for every tool rather than expressing the restriction where it belongs.

questions.q: A PreToolUse hook needs to apply a stricter rate limit to tool calls made by subagents than to calls made from the main thread, and it needs to tell the two apart purely from fields already present on the hook input. Which fields let it do that?
options: The agent_id and agent_type fields, present on PreToolUseHookInput when the call originates inside a subagent.
The session_id field combined with the cwd field, since subagents always run from a completely different working directory.
The parent_tool_use_id field, which is populated only for calls issued from the main thread rather than a subagent.
The permission_mode field, since subagents always run under a noticeably stricter permission mode than the main thread does.
questions.explain: agent_id and agent_type appear on PreToolUseHookInput specifically when a call originates inside a subagent, which is exactly the signal needed to apply a different rate limit there. session_id and cwd don't reliably distinguish the two contexts, parent_tool_use_id doesn't work the way described, and permission_mode is not tied to whether a call came from a subagent.

knowledgePoints.name: Command hooks and exit codes
knowledgePoints.teach:
Hooks can also be shell commands configured in settings files rather than callbacks in your code. For those:

  • Exit code 2 blocks the action and feeds stderr back to Claude.
  • Stderr from a hook that exits 0 goes only to the debug log — Claude never sees it.

That second rule explains a common confusion: "my hook printed a warning and the model ignored it." It did not ignore it. It never received it.

questions.q: A command hook configured for PreToolUse prints a warning to stderr reading 'this path is outside the project root' and then exits with code 0. The team expects Claude to see the warning and reconsider the file path, but across several transcripts the model never reacts to it. What explains this?
options: The warning is delivered to Claude directly, but as a system message the model is trained to treat as low priority.
The tool call is blocked before it runs, so there is nothing left for the model to react to in the first place.
Exit code 0 tells the framework the hook succeeded, so stderr goes only to the debug log and Claude never sees it.
stderr from a command hook is injected beside the tool result only when the matcher targets exactly one tool.
questions.explain: Exit code 0 tells the framework the hook finished normally, so any stderr it wrote is recorded only in the debug log and never reaches Claude. The call is not blocked, since blocking requires exit code 2, and stderr delivery to Claude does not depend on how narrowly the matcher is scoped.

questions.q: Your command hook needs to stop a dangerous Bash command from executing at all, and it needs its stderr message delivered back to Claude so the model can adjust its approach on the next attempt. Which exit code should the hook script return?
options: Exit code 0, which signals to the framework that the hook actively intervened in the tool call.
Exit code 1, which is reserved specifically for blocking actions along with a spoken reason.
Any non-zero exit code, since the framework treats all of them identically as a deliberate block.
Exit code 2, which blocks the action from running and feeds the hook's stderr back to Claude.
questions.explain: Exit code 2 is the specific signal that blocks the action and feeds the hook's stderr back to Claude so it can adjust course. Exit 0 means the hook succeeded and the action proceeds, exit 1 has no special meaning here, and other non-zero codes are treated as the hook itself having failed rather than as a deliberate block.

reviewQuestions.q: You are configuring a HookMatcher and need to know how long the framework waits before treating your callback as timed out, given you set no explicit timeout value. Your hook is registered under PreToolUse, and a teammate's hook is registered under UserPromptSubmit. What are the applicable defaults?
options: PreToolUse defaults to 600 seconds, while UserPromptSubmit defaults to 30 seconds since a user is waiting.
Both default to 30 seconds, since that is the single standard timeout applied across every hook event.
There is no default timeout at all; every HookMatcher must specify one explicitly or registration fails.
Both default to 600 seconds across every event, except Stop hooks, which fall back to 30 seconds instead.
reviewQuestions.explain: The default hook timeout is 600 seconds, except for UserPromptSubmit, which defaults to 30 seconds specifically because a user is sitting there waiting on the response. There is a default even when none is set explicitly, and it is not a flat 30 or 600 seconds across every event.

knowledgePoints.name: Out vs. back
knowledgePoints.teach:
PreToolUse guards what goes out. PostToolUse cleans what comes back.

Direction is the whole distinction, and it decides almost every hook question on the exam. Two named patterns:

  • Tool call interception hook (glossary t11) — intercepts an outgoing call to enforce a business rule. Canonical case: block process_refund over $500 and redirect to human escalation. That is PreToolUse with permissionDecision: "deny" and a reason — or updatedInput to rewrite it.
  • PostToolUse normalization (t10) — intercepts results to transform them before the model reads them. Canonical case: several MCP tools return timestamps in different formats (Unix epoch, ISO 8601, MM/DD/YYYY) and a hook normalises them so the model never has to reconcile the mismatch.

questions.q: Three MCP tools your agent calls return timestamps in three different formats — one as Unix epoch, one as ISO 8601, and one as MM/DD/YYYY — and the model occasionally miscalculates date comparisons because it has to reconcile the mismatch itself. Where should you fix this?
options: In the system prompt, listing each tool's timestamp format so the model can interpret every value correctly.
In a PostToolUse hook that normalizes each tool's returned timestamp into a single consistent format.
In a PreToolUse hook that rewrites the outgoing arguments before each of the three tool calls runs.
By merging the three tools into a single wrapper tool that always returns results as Unix epoch.
questions.explain: Reconciling inconsistent tool output is exactly what PostToolUse normalization is for — the hook rewrites each returned timestamp into one consistent format so the model never has to compare formats itself. Explaining the formats in the system prompt still leaves the reconciliation work to the model, a PreToolUse hook only touches the outgoing request rather than what comes back, and merging the tools is a much larger change than the problem requires.

questions.q: Your finance team requires that any process_refund call for more than $500 never actually execute — it must be intercepted and routed to a human reviewer before the payment provider is ever contacted. Which hook should implement this?
options: A PostToolUse hook that checks the refund amount in the completed result and reverses it if it exceeds $500.
A UserPromptSubmit hook that rejects any user message mentioning refunds over $500 before the agent responds.
A Stop hook that refuses to let the agent end its current turn until a human has reviewed any large refund it issued.
A PreToolUse hook that denies the outgoing process_refund call and supplies a reason when the amount exceeds $500.
questions.explain: Blocking the refund before it ever reaches the payment provider requires intercepting the outgoing call, which is what a PreToolUse hook denying process_refund with a reason accomplishes. A PostToolUse check would only notice the refund after it has already happened, a UserPromptSubmit hook can't inspect the tool call itself, and a Stop hook would let the refund go through and only block the agent from finishing afterward.

reviewQuestions.q: A new team member is trying to decide, as a general rule and without inspecting each case individually, whether a given hook requirement belongs on PreToolUse or PostToolUse. Which rule correctly captures the distinction?
options: PreToolUse guards what goes out to a tool before it runs; PostToolUse handles what comes back from it afterward.
PreToolUse is reserved for cheap, fast checks; PostToolUse is for checks that are expensive to compute.
PreToolUse only applies to MCP tools; PostToolUse only applies to built-in tools like Read and Write.
PreToolUse can block a call outright, while PostToolUse can only observe the result and log it.
reviewQuestions.explain: PreToolUse sits before the tool runs and guards the outgoing call, while PostToolUse sits after and handles what comes back — that direction, not cost or tool type, is the actual distinction. PreToolUse isn't limited to MCP tools, and PostToolUse is not observe-only: it can also block via a decision field of its own.

knowledgePoints.name: Two return shapes, split by event
knowledgePoints.teach:
EventsPatternKey fields
PreToolUsehookSpecificOutputpermissionDecision: allow / deny / ask / defer, plus permissionDecisionReason
PostToolUse, PostToolUseFailure, UserPromptSubmit, Stop, SubagentStop, PreCompacttop-level decisiondecision: "block", reason
PermissionRequesthookSpecificOutputdecision.behavior: allow / deny
SessionStart, SubagentStartcontext onlyadditionalContext; no blocking
Notification, SessionEnd, PostCompact, InstructionsLoadednoneside effects only — logging, cleanup

Getting the shape wrong is silent: a PostToolUse hook that returns permissionDecision is returning a field that event does not read.

questions.q: You write a PostToolUse hook that inspects a completed database write and, wanting to prevent the model from seeing the result, returns hookSpecificOutput.permissionDecision: "deny". After deploying it, the questionable result still reaches the model unchanged. Why?
options: The tool result is discarded silently before the model ever receives it, leaving the model working from stale data.
PostToolUse reads a top-level decision field, not hookSpecificOutput.permissionDecision, so the field is ignored.
The tool call is automatically retried once with the exact same arguments, producing the identical result again.
Returning a field that this particular event does not expect raises a validation error that halts the entire run.
questions.explain: PostToolUse reads a top-level decision field rather than hookSpecificOutput.permissionDecision, so returning the PreToolUse-shaped field is simply ignored and the result reaches the model unchanged. Nothing is discarded, retried, or flagged as a validation error — the mismatch fails silently rather than loudly.

questions.q: You need to inject a short piece of context into the conversation right at the moment a new session or a new subagent begins, knowing these particular hooks cannot block anything since nothing has happened yet. Which pair of events are you working with?
options: PreToolUse and PostToolUse, which both surround individual tool calls rather than whole sessions.
Stop and SubagentStop, which fire only once the current turn is already in the process of ending.
SessionStart and SubagentStart, which fire before anything exists yet and can only add additionalContext.
PermissionRequest and PreCompact, which both gate an action that is already underway in the current tool call.
questions.explain: SessionStart and SubagentStart fire before anything has happened yet for that session or subagent, so all they can do is add additionalContext rather than block a call. PreToolUse and PostToolUse concern individual tool calls rather than session start, and Stop, SubagentStop, and PermissionRequest all fire at points where something is already underway.

knowledgePoints.name: The four PreToolUse decisions
knowledgePoints.teach:
permissionDecision takes four values, and they are not two pairs:

  • allow — proceed, skipping the rest of the permission flow.
  • deny — refuse, with permissionDecisionReason fed back so the model can adapt rather than retry blindly.
  • ask — fall through to the normal prompt / canUseTool.
  • defer — park the call and hand it to your application.

Always supply permissionDecisionReason on a deny. A denial without a reason teaches the model nothing, and it will usually try again.

questions.q: A PreToolUse hook denies a call to send_email because the recipient address is outside the allowed domain, but the hook's author leaves permissionDecisionReason empty. Over the following turns, the model repeatedly retries the same call with only cosmetic changes to the arguments. Why does supplying a reason on a deny matter?
options: The reason is fed back to the model, giving it the information it needs to adapt instead of retrying blindly.
permissionDecisionReason is a required field, and omitting it causes the SDK to silently ignore the deny.
The reason text is recorded in billing and usage records so the team can audit denied calls later on.
Without a reason string present, the framework does not honor the exit code the hook returned.
questions.explain: permissionDecisionReason is what gets fed back to the model, giving it the specific information needed to adapt its next attempt instead of retrying the same call with cosmetic changes. It is not a required field that would break the deny if omitted, it has nothing to do with billing records, and the exit code's effect does not depend on whether a reason string is present.

questions.q: A PreToolUse hook you are writing has no strong opinion on whether a particular Bash call should be allowed, and you want the decision to fall through to whatever the normal permission prompt or canUseTool callback would otherwise decide. Which permissionDecision value expresses that?
options: allow, since it lets the tool call proceed immediately, skipping any further permission checks entirely.
ask, since it hands the decision back to the normal permission flow instead of deciding itself.
deny, since it forces the decision back to the user through an explanatory error message right away.
defer, since it parks the call for your own application to resolve at some later point in time.
questions.explain: ask is the value that explicitly hands the decision back to the normal permission flow when the hook itself has no opinion. allow would let the call through unconditionally, deny would refuse it outright, and defer would park it for your own application to resolve rather than deferring to the built-in flow.

reviewQuestions.q: You are writing a Stop hook that must prevent the agent from ending its turn until its response includes at least one citation. Which field on the hook's return value actually accomplishes that?
options: Returning exit code 2 from a command-line script registered specifically on the Stop event.
Setting additionalContext to a string that explains a citation is required before finishing.
Setting a top-level decision field to "block" along with a reason, the pattern Stop shares with PostToolUse.
Setting hookSpecificOutput.permissionDecision to "deny", the field a PreToolUse hook would use.
reviewQuestions.explain: Stop belongs to the family of events that use a top-level decision field set to "block" with a reason, the same pattern PostToolUse uses. hookSpecificOutput.permissionDecision belongs to PreToolUse instead, additionalContext alone can't prevent the turn from ending, and a command hook's exit code is a mechanism for shell-based hooks rather than the field being asked about here.

knowledgePoints.name: updatedInput and additionalContext
knowledgePoints.teach:
Denial is not the only move. Two fields let a hook fix instead of refuse:

  • PreToolUse → updatedInput (directly under hookSpecificOutput) replaces the tool's arguments before it runs. Use it when the call is nearly right — a missing tenant filter, an unscoped path, a limit that is too high.
  • PostToolUse → additionalContext injects a string into Claude's context, wrapped in a system reminder, placed next to the tool result. Capped at 10,000 characters; longer output is written to a file and replaced with a preview and the path.

Rewriting is usually kinder than denying: the model gets a working result rather than a rejection it has to reason its way around.

questions.q: Your agent repeatedly calls a search_records tool without the required tenant_id filter, which would let it read across tenant boundaries if the results were ever returned to the model. The call is otherwise well-formed and clearly intends to search within the current tenant. Should a PreToolUse hook deny the call or rewrite it?
options: Deny it with a reason so the model learns the rule and adds the filter itself on its next attempt.
Remove the search_records tool from the agent's available toolset entirely, so this can never recur.
Let the call proceed and catch the cross-tenant leak afterward inside a PostToolUse hook instead.
Rewrite the call with updatedInput, adding the missing tenant_id filter before it is allowed to proceed.
questions.explain: The call is nearly right — it's missing one filter — so rewriting it with updatedInput closes the gap immediately and lets the search still complete successfully. Denying costs a turn while the model retries, removing the tool entirely is a disproportionate response to a fixable mistake, and catching the leak in PostToolUse would mean the cross-tenant read already happened.

questions.q: A PostToolUse hook you wrote injects a long diagnostic report into additionalContext after every deploy-status check, and one particular report happens to run to roughly 40,000 characters. What happens to the injected context in that case?
options: It is capped at 1,000 characters, and the remainder beyond that is truncated silently with no other notice.
It is capped at 10,000 characters, with the overflow written to a file and a preview left in context.
It is capped at 100,000 tokens, a limit well above the size of this particular report, so nothing unusual happens.
There is no cap on additionalContext at all, so the full 40,000-character report is passed through unchanged.
questions.explain: additionalContext is capped at 10,000 characters, and content beyond that limit is written to a file with a preview and the file path left in context instead of being lost. The other caps and the claim of no cap at all don't match how the framework actually handles oversized context.

reviewQuestions.q: A PreToolUse hook needs to silently correct a tool call's arguments — for example, clamping a limit parameter that is set too high — rather than deny the call outright. Which field on the hook's response carries the corrected arguments?
options: additionalContext, the same field a PostToolUse hook uses to inject extra information afterward.
updatedPermissions, a field that instead adjusts what the tool is allowed to do going forward.
updatedInput, nested directly under hookSpecificOutput, which replaces the tool's arguments before it runs.
permissionDecisionReason, which explains a deny but carries no replacement arguments of its own.
reviewQuestions.explain: updatedInput, nested under hookSpecificOutput on a PreToolUse response, is exactly the field that replaces a tool's arguments before it runs, which is what a silent correction like clamping a limit requires. additionalContext only applies after a tool has already run, updatedPermissions changes future authorization rather than this call's arguments, and permissionDecisionReason only explains a deny.

knowledgePoints.name: Parking a call for a human
knowledgePoints.teach:
A PreToolUse hook returning permissionDecision: "defer" produces:

  • stop_reason: "tool_deferred"
  • the pending call in deferred_tool_use

That is how you surface an approval request in your own UI — a manager approving a refund in your web app, not in a terminal — and resume later with the same session_id.

Contrast with ask, which hands the decision to the SDK's own permission flow, and with deny, which ends the matter.

questions.q: Your company requires that any refund over $1,000 be approved by a manager inside your own web application — not through a terminal prompt — before the refund tool actually executes, with the run resuming automatically once approval is granted. Which permissionDecision value should the PreToolUse hook return?
options: deny, along with a clear reason explaining that manager approval is required before this can proceed.
ask, which routes the decision to the SDK's own built-in interactive permission flow instead.
allow, and then reverse the refund transaction afterward if the manager ends up rejecting it.
defer, which hands the pending call to your application to surface and resolve on its own.
questions.explain: defer is built for exactly this situation: it parks the pending call and hands it to your own application to surface and resolve, resuming the run once approval comes back. deny would end the matter without a path to approval, ask would route to the SDK's own permission UI rather than your web app, and allow-then-reverse would let the refund execute before anyone had approved it.

questions.q: After a PreToolUse hook returns permissionDecision: "defer" for a pending refund call, your backend needs to detect that the call is now waiting on external approval rather than assuming the turn simply ended normally. What should it check for?
options: A stop_reason value of "tool_deferred", with the pending call itself available in deferred_tool_use.
A stop_reason value of "end_turn", the same value used whenever the agent finishes a turn normally.
A stop_reason value of "max_turns", indicating the run has hit its configured turn limit.
A stop_reason value of "tool_use", the generic value returned whenever any tool call occurs at all.
questions.explain: A defer decision produces a distinct stop_reason of "tool_deferred", with the pending call itself available in deferred_tool_use so the backend knows exactly what is waiting on approval. "end_turn", "max_turns", and "tool_use" are all used for other situations and would not signal that a call is parked awaiting external approval.

reviewQuestions.q: A manager has just approved a refund that was parked by a defer decision, and you need the agent's run to continue exactly where it left off rather than starting the conversation over from scratch. How do you resume it?
options: Start an entirely new query using the same prompt text that originally triggered the deferred call.
Re-run the PreToolUse hook that produced the defer decision so it can re-evaluate the call again.
Resume the run using the same session_id that was active at the moment the call was deferred.
Call the underlying refund tool yourself and inject its result directly into the transcript.
reviewQuestions.explain: Resuming with the same session_id that was active when the call was deferred picks the run back up exactly where it stopped. Starting a new query loses that state, re-running the hook would just produce another defer decision, and calling the tool yourself bypasses the approval flow the defer was designed to enforce.

knowledgePoints.name: Six modes
knowledgePoints.teach:
ModeBehaviour
defaultStandard prompting behaviour
acceptEditsAuto-accept file edits
planRead-only; explore and propose without editing
dontAskNever prompt — deny anything not pre-approved
bypassPermissionsSkip checks (explicit ask rules still prompt); requires allowDangerouslySkipPermissions: true
autoA model classifier approves or denies what would have been prompts

The pair worth drilling is dontAsk versus bypassPermissions: one denies everything unapproved, the other allows almost everything. They sound similar and are opposites.

questions.q: You are configuring an unattended agent that runs every night with no one watching it, and the requirement is strict: it must never prompt for permission, and it must never perform any action that was not explicitly pre-approved in advance. Which permission mode satisfies both requirements?
options: auto, since a model classifier approves or denies actions on your behalf without ever prompting.
acceptEdits, since it silently approves file edits without ever showing an interactive prompt.
bypassPermissions, since it skips permission checks and lets nearly everything through unprompted.
dontAsk, since it never prompts and denies anything that was not explicitly pre-approved.
questions.explain: dontAsk is built for exactly this case: it never prompts, and anything that was not explicitly pre-approved is denied rather than allowed. auto still lets a classifier approve actions on its own judgment, acceptEdits only concerns file edits specifically, and bypassPermissions also never prompts but does so by allowing nearly everything rather than denying it.

questions.q: Your team enables bypassPermissions for a coding agent to avoid interrupting it with prompts, but a scoped disallow rule like "Bash(rm *)" still blocks a destructive command the agent later attempts. This surprises a teammate who assumed bypass mode skipped every check. What does bypassPermissions actually still honor?
options: Explicit ask rules and scoped disallow rules, both of which still take effect even under bypass mode.
Nothing at all; bypassPermissions is designed to skip every permission check without any exception.
Only the allowedTools list, which continues to auto-approve the specific tools it names.
Hooks still fire under bypassPermissions, but none of the ordinary permission rules apply anymore.
questions.explain: bypassPermissions still honors explicit ask rules and scoped disallow rules like "Bash(rm *)", which is why the destructive command was still blocked. It does not skip every check without exception, its effect isn't limited to policing the allowedTools list, and hooks continuing to fire is a separate mechanism from the permission rules being described here.

reviewQuestions.q: Two modes, dontAsk and bypassPermissions, both run without ever showing an interactive prompt, and a teammate assumes that makes them interchangeable. Which statement correctly distinguishes their default behavior toward an unapproved action?
options: dontAsk allows everything through by default, while bypassPermissions denies anything unapproved.
dontAsk denies anything that was not pre-approved, while bypassPermissions allows it through instead.
Both modes skip prompts and allow whatever action is requested, with no real difference between them.
They are two configuration names that both map to exactly the same underlying permission behavior.
reviewQuestions.explain: dontAsk denies anything that wasn't pre-approved, while bypassPermissions allows nearly everything through — same silence, opposite defaults. Neither the reversed version nor the claim that both allow everything nor the claim that they're identical describes the actual difference between the two modes.

knowledgePoints.name: canUseTool only fires on a prompt
knowledgePoints.teach:
canUseTool is the SDK replacement for the interactive permission prompt. It is invoked only when the permission flow resolves to a prompt.

Calls already approved by allowedTools, by a settings allow rule, or by a permissive permissionMode (acceptEdits, bypassPermissions) never reach it.

To gate every tool call unconditionally, use a PreToolUse hook, not canUseTool.

Exceptions that reach canUseTool even when otherwise allowed: AskUserQuestion, MCP tools marked requiresUserInteraction, and connector tools an organisation set to ask. In dontAsk mode those are denied instead of prompting.

It returns a PermissionResult: { behavior: "allow", updatedInput?, updatedPermissions? } or { behavior: "deny", message, interrupt? }.

questions.q: You add logging inside your canUseTool callback expecting it to capture every tool call the agent makes, but comparing the log against the full transcript afterward shows a large number of calls are missing. What explains the gap?
options: canUseTool calls are sampled rather than invoked on every single call once tool-call volume gets high enough.
Only MCP tools are ever routed through the canUseTool callback, while built-in tools bypass it entirely.
Logging placed inside canUseTool has to be made asynchronous, or entries can get silently dropped somewhere.
Calls already auto-approved by allowedTools, a settings rule, or a permissive mode never reach canUseTool.
questions.explain: Calls that are already auto-approved — by allowedTools, a settings allow rule, or a permissive mode like bypassPermissions — never reach canUseTool at all, which is exactly why the log has gaps. canUseTool isn't sampled, it isn't restricted to MCP tools, and an async logging bug wouldn't produce gaps that line up with which calls were pre-approved.

questions.q: Your agent runs under bypassPermissions mode, and you assume canUseTool will never fire for anything since the mode is designed to skip prompts entirely. During testing, though, it does still fire for one particular kind of call. Which of these correctly reaches canUseTool even when otherwise allowed?
options: An AskUserQuestion call, which reaches canUseTool in any mode, including bypassPermissions.
A Bash call, whenever Bash happens to be explicitly listed in the agent's allowedTools configuration.
A Read call, specifically whenever it happens to run under acceptEdits mode instead of default mode.
Any tool call at all, simply because the agent happens to be running under bypassPermissions mode.
questions.explain: AskUserQuestion is one of the exceptions that reaches canUseTool in every permission mode, including bypassPermissions, regardless of what would otherwise be allowed. Being listed in allowedTools or running under acceptEdits or bypassPermissions is exactly what causes other calls to skip canUseTool rather than reach it.

reviewQuestions.q: You are deciding where to put audit logging that must record every single tool call the agent makes with no gaps, and a teammate suggests putting it inside canUseTool since that is the SDK's permission callback. Why is that the wrong place, given when each mechanism fires?
options: canUseTool fires on every tool call without exception, while PreToolUse only fires for file-write tools.
canUseTool fires only when the permission flow resolves to a prompt, while a PreToolUse hook fires on every call.
They fire at exactly the same point for exactly the same set of calls, so either placement works equally well.
PreToolUse only fires under default permission mode, while canUseTool fires regardless of the mode in use.
reviewQuestions.explain: canUseTool only fires when the permission flow actually resolves to a prompt, so any call that gets auto-approved never reaches it — a PreToolUse hook, by contrast, fires on every call regardless of how it will ultimately be decided. The claims that canUseTool fires on everything, that the two fire identically, or that PreToolUse is mode-restricted all get the relationship backwards.

knowledgePoints.name: allowedTools auto-approves; it does not restrict
knowledgePoints.teach:
allowedTools does not restrict.

It auto-approves the tools it lists. Unlisted tools do not become unavailable — they fall through to permissionMode and canUseTool. Depending on the mode, an unlisted tool may prompt, be denied, or simply run.

To actually block, use disallowedTools, which has two modes of its own:

  • A bare "Bash" removes the tool from Claude's context entirely — it is not in the tool list, so it is never considered.
  • A scoped rule like "Bash(rm *)" leaves the tool available and denies matching calls in every mode, including bypassPermissions.

questions.q: You configure allowedTools to contain only Read and Grep, running the agent under default permission mode, expecting this to prevent it from ever writing a file. Partway through a session, the agent successfully calls Write after a permission prompt appears and you approve it. What does this reveal about allowedTools?
options: allowedTools should have acted as a strict whitelist, so this behavior indicates a bug in the permission system.
allowedTools should have removed Write from the agent's available tools entirely, so this call should have been impossible.
allowedTools only auto-approves the tools it lists; Write, being unlisted, correctly fell through to the normal permission mode.
A hook must have explicitly allowed the write, since allowedTools alone can never let an unlisted call through.
questions.explain: allowedTools only auto-approves the tools it names; an unlisted tool like Write doesn't become unavailable, it simply falls through to whatever the active permission mode does with it, which in default mode is a prompt. It is not a whitelist, it does not remove unlisted tools from the agent's context, and no hook was needed to explain a prompt that the permission mode itself would produce.

questions.q: You need a rule that keeps the Bash tool available to the agent for legitimate use, but reliably denies any Bash call matching rm *, even in configurations where the agent runs under bypassPermissions mode for everything else. Which configuration achieves that?
options: disallowedTools: ["Bash(rm *)"], a scoped rule keeping Bash available but denying matches in every mode.
allowedTools: ["Read"], since leaving Bash off the allow list should be sufficient to block its destructive calls entirely.
permissionMode: "plan", which prevents any tool anywhere from executing changes regardless of which tools are listed.
A canUseTool callback that returns deny for matching commands, since it fires for every single Bash call no matter the mode.
questions.explain: A scoped rule like disallowedTools: ["Bash(rm *)"] leaves Bash available for legitimate use while still denying matching calls in every mode, including bypassPermissions. Leaving Bash out of allowedTools wouldn't remove it under a permissive mode, permissionMode: "plan" is a blanket read-only mode rather than a targeted rule, and canUseTool would never even fire for a call already allowed under bypassPermissions.

reviewQuestions.q: You are choosing between disallowedTools: ["Bash"] and disallowedTools: ["Bash(rm *)"] to restrict a coding agent, and need to know exactly how the two differ in effect before picking one. Which statement correctly describes the difference?
options: There is no real difference between them at all; the scoped version is simply a more specific way to write the same rule.
The bare tool name removes Bash from the agent's context entirely, while the scoped rule keeps it available but polices calls.
The bare tool name causes a prompt on every single Bash call, while the scoped rule denies matching calls outright without ever prompting.
The scoped rule only takes effect when the agent runs under default permission mode, unlike the bare tool-name rule.
reviewQuestions.explain: The bare tool name removes Bash from the agent's context entirely, so it is never available to call, while the scoped rule keeps Bash usable but denies specifically the matching calls. Neither one merely prompts instead of denying, they are not equivalent to each other, and the scoped rule's effect isn't limited to default permission mode.
